name: Gareth Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work a stamping press at Corran Steel, a plant that makes brackets and uprights for warehouse shelving. A stamping press is a big machine that punches flat steel sheet into shape with a die, which is like a heavy metal cookie cutter. I feed the sheet, keep my hands clear of the guard, and stack the brackets in cages. I'm still learning the die changes, and I need the setter's help for the bigger ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home with you, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's loud and it's repetitive, but the people are good. I like the rhythm when it's going well, bang, stack, bang, stack. I've used one of those AI chat apps a couple of times to write a CV and once to explain my payslip, but not for the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought it would change much. At work the lads would say the same. I might share a funny post about it, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, warehouses keep getting built, so people keep needing shelving. As long as that's true, my job on the stamping press stays my job. I've got about four months saved and I share the flat with Owen, my mate, so the rent's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to learn the big die changes myself, so I don't need the setter every time. I'd keep saving a bit each month, maybe towards a car. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you about Corran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overtime, mainly. In the quiet months they cut Saturday shifts, and that's where the extra money comes from. It's annoying, but it's not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra money if overtime stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a second-hand car, so I'm not getting two buses to work. Owen keeps telling me to save for a deposit instead. He's probably right, but a car feels more real.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, I never expected much to change.
I might share **a funny post** online, nothing more.
think: Privately, my job **stays my job**, because warehouses keep needing shelving.
With **four months saved** and shared rent, I'm in decent shape.
do: Learn the **big die changes** so I don't need the setter each time.
Save a bit **each month** towards a second-hand car.
Carry on as normal with **no big changes**.
S0.quote: Warehouses keep getting built, so people keep needing shelving. As long as that's true, my job on the stamping press stays my job.
fieldNote: His security comes from **steady demand** for warehouse shelving.
His only niggle is **Saturday overtime** being cut in quiet months.
He has tried AI for a CV and **a payslip**, never for work.

steps.text: Learn the big die changes on the stamping press himself
Save each month towards a second-hand car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that'll feel it, not us on the presses. I'd say robots are expensive and we're cheap, which is a sad thing to say out loud. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's fine for a few years, then it isn't. The office at Corran would shrink, and they'd start looking at the press line with robot arms. They already have one robot on the welding cell, and it's never off sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained on the welding robot, because I'd rather be the person minding it than the person it replaces. I'd try the AI app more, to understand the robot manuals and the safety stuff. I'd keep saving, maybe skip the car for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but it's there in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are expensive and you're cheap. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's true and it's a bit depressing. I'm on typical pay for the job, and for now that makes me worth keeping. But the robot gets cheaper every year and I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about the welding robot training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia, the shift manager. She's fair, and she likes people who ask. I'd go to her on a Monday when she's in a good mood, not a Friday.

say: I'd say **the office** feels it first, not the presses.
I'd admit robots are expensive and **we're cheap**, sadly.
think: Privately, it's fine for **a few years**, then it isn't.
The **welding robot** at Corran is never off sick, and that's the warning.
do: Ask Kasia (my shift manager) for **welding robot training**.
Use the **AI app** more to understand robot manuals and safety rules.
Keep saving and **put off the car** for now.
feel: **Uneasy**, not panicking but always in the back of my head.
S1.quote: I'm on typical pay for the job, and for now that makes me worth keeping. But the robot gets cheaper every year and I don't.
fieldNote: He sees the **cost race** between himself and a robot clearly.
His plan is to become **the robot minder** rather than the replaced worker.
He'd wait to try new tools until **the job requires it**, then commit.

steps.text: Ask Kasia for training on the welding robot cell
Use the AI app to read the robot manuals and safety rules
Keep saving and put off buying the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going way too fast and someone should hit the brakes. At work everyone would be talking about it at break, half joking, half not. I'd probably share news stories about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AI part in 2028 doesn't touch me much, but the robots in 2031 do. Pressing and stacking is exactly what robots will do first. I'm junior and I still need help with die changes, so I'd be early on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the car fund and push savings up to six months, starting this month. I'd look for a job that's harder for robots, like fitting shelving on site instead of making it, because every warehouse is a different shape. In the first year after AGI, I'd try to get a fitting job before the factory starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having three years before the robots come change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got time to switch, but not much. If I sit on it, I'll be one of fifty press operators all applying for the same thing. If I start looking now, I could be fitting shelving by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Owen say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen works in a call centre, so the AI part hits him first, in 2028. He'd probably be out before me. We'd have to talk about whether we can keep the flat.

say: I'd say it's going **way too fast** and someone should brake.
I'd **share news stories** and join the half-joking talk at break.
think: Privately, the **robots in 2031** hit me harder than AI in 2028.
Being **junior** and needing help with die changes puts me early on the list.
do: Stop the car fund and push savings to **six months** this month.
Look for **shelving fitter** jobs on site, harder for robots.
Move to a **fitting job** before the factory starts cutting.
S2.quote: If I sit on it, I'll be one of fifty press operators all applying for the same thing. If I start looking now, I could be fitting shelving by 2029.
fieldNote: He reasons clearly that **site work** is harder for robots than factory work.
His flatmate Owen (a call centre worker) is **exposed sooner**, putting the flat at risk.
The three-year gap gives him **a head start** if he moves first.

steps.text: Stop the car fund and build savings to six months
Apply for on-site shelving fitter jobs with installers
Drop nights out and keep spending to rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and we should use it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to learn something extra now. Online I'd share stuff about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 still take the press job, but five years gives me time to get a trade. I'd be about thirty-five, still young enough to start somewhere new. It's scary, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start looking at installation work and maybe a forklift licence, which helps on site. In a couple of years I'd move to a shelving installer full-time. I'd keep saving and probably still buy a cheap car, because fitters drive to jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a workable kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a forklift licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On site you're moving pallets of uprights around all day. Fitters with a licence get picked first, Kasia told me once. It's a few hundred quid and a week of evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the installers start using robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble again, but later. Every warehouse is a different shape, so I think fitting shelving is one of the last bits to go. I'm not sure, though, nobody really knows.

say: I'd say five years is **a fair warning** to use.
I'd tell younger lads to **learn something extra** now.
think: Privately, robots by **2034** still take the press job.
Five years is time to **get a trade** while I'm around thirty-five.
do: Get a **forklift licence** this year for a few hundred quid.
Move to a **shelving installer** full-time within a couple of years.
Buy **a cheap car**, because fitters drive to jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, but a workable kind of anxious.
S3.quote: Every warehouse is a different shape, so I think fitting shelving is one of the last bits to go. I'm not sure, though, nobody really knows.
fieldNote: He builds a **stepwise switch** from press to site fitting.
He admits **uncertainty** about whether site work stays safe.
Kasia's tip about **forklift licences** shapes his first step.

steps.text: Pay for a forklift licence over a week of evenings
Apply to shelving installers within two years
Buy a cheap second-hand car for driving to fitting jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and things will sort themselves out. At work we'd mostly forget about it after a week. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the press job still goes around 2039, but I'd be thirty-nine and hopefully long gone from it. Ten years is enough to get a proper trade, maybe even electrician. That's the honest upside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Corran a couple more years and save. Then I'd try for an electrical apprenticeship, even if it's a pay cut for a while. I'd buy the car this year, since there's no rush on everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but only a bit. It's far enough away that I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really take a pay cut for an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I've got four or five months saved, yes. Owen says I'd moan about it the whole time. I probably would, but I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long time make you more relaxed than you should be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. The lads at work would forget about it in a week, and so might I. I'd need a date on the calendar to make myself move.

say: I'd say ten years is long and **things will sort out**.
At work we'd **forget about it** after a week.
think: Privately, the press job still goes around **2039**.
Ten years is enough for **a proper trade**, maybe electrician.
do: Stay at Corran **a couple more years** and keep saving.
Apply for an **electrical apprenticeship**, accepting a pay cut.
Buy **the car** this year, since there's less rush.
feel: **Mildly anxious**, but far enough away to plan.
S4.quote: The lads at work would forget about it in a week, and so might I. I'd need a date on the calendar to make myself move.
fieldNote: He knows a long deadline could make him **too relaxed**.
He'd accept **a pay cut** for an apprenticeship if savings allow.
His job still goes in the end, so his **income risk** stays real.

steps.text: Stay on the Corran presses for two more years
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship after building savings
Buy a second-hand car this year
Save towards four or five months before the apprenticeship

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots come in 2031 and I'd be one of fifty press operators all looking for the same jobs. What would help is cheap courses for things like forklift and electrical, and firms telling us early when robots are coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who share a flat. If my flatmate Owen loses his call centre job first, my rent doubles, and that's a robot problem I didn't even have yet.

headlineQuote: If my flatmate Owen loses his call centre job first, my rent doubles, and that's a robot problem I didn't even have yet.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old stamping press operator** at a shelving plant, still learning die changes.
He shares a flat with **Owen (his flatmate)**, a call centre worker, and has about four months saved.
He's **pragmatic**, tries AI apps now and then, and moves once he sees a clear path.
His plan is to leave the press for **site fitting** or an electrical trade.
He's calm with no change, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and anxious with more warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots by 2031 leaving him in a crowd of press operators chasing jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **forklift** and electrical courses, and firms giving **early warning** of robots.
